title: TCS Chairman Says Half a Million AI Agents Will Join the Workforce Within Three Years. Mass Hiring Is Over.
excerpt: N Chandrasekaran's prediction at the annual meeting sent TCS stock tumbling and forced India's entire IT sector to confront a question it has been avoiding.
body:
The chairman of India's largest IT company stood before shareholders on Tuesday and said something the industry has been dreading for years. Mass hiring, the engine that turned Tata Consultancy Services into a $150 billion enterprise and pulled millions of Indian families into the middle class, is winding down.

"If the company has half a million employees, the day is not far when the company will have half a million AI agents," N Chandrasekaran told TCS's 31st annual general meeting. "The company will not be hiring the kind of numbers it used to hire."

The timeline, he said, is three years.

## The Numbers Behind the Shift

TCS ended fiscal year 2026 with 584,519 employees — a net reduction of roughly 23,500 from the previous year. The company had originally projected losing about 1,200 workers. It shed more than twenty times that estimate.

Last July alone, TCS cut 12,000 positions. And yet Chandrasekaran insists the company is not planning layoffs. What it is doing, he said, is replacing the conveyor belt. The era of onboarding tens of thousands of fresh graduates each year — the factory model that defined Indian IT for three decades — is ending.

In its place, TCS is building what Chandrasekaran calls an "AI-first delivery model." AI revenue reached an annualised $2.5 billion in the March quarter, growing at a compound quarterly rate of 22.4 per cent. The company says more than 570,000 of its employees are now "AI-ready," having completed training through internal platforms and partnerships like LinkedIn Learning.

## An Industry-Wide Reckoning

Chandrasekaran's comments carry weight far beyond TCS. India's IT services sector is worth $315 billion and remains one of the country's largest private employers. Infosys, Wipro, HCL Technologies, and Tech Mahindra all face the same structural pressure: clients want AI-driven efficiency, not headcount-driven billing.

The Nifty IT index has fallen 25 per cent in 2026. TCS itself has dropped more than 32 per cent. One trading session in early June saw TCS lose nearly 8 per cent of its market value in a single day as investors digested the implications of Chandrasekaran's AI-agent prediction.

The broader concern is straightforward. India's IT industry built its moat on a simple premise — highly skilled engineers at a fraction of Western labour costs. If AI agents can perform the same work at a fraction of even Indian labour costs, that moat disappears.

"Some of the work being done will go to AI agents," Chandrasekaran said. "That will be the nature of the transition that we have to go through not only as a company, as an industry, and as a country."

## What This Means for the Diaspora

For the hundreds of thousands of Indian IT professionals working in the United States, the United Kingdom, and Canada on H-1B and Tier 2 visas, the implications run deep. Many arrived on contracts staffed through exactly the kind of body-shopping model that AI now threatens to render obsolete.

The pressure is coming from both sides. In the US, the Trump administration's $100,000 H-1B fee — recently struck down by a federal court but already being legislated by Congress through the PROTECT Act — was designed to make importing foreign tech workers prohibitively expensive. Now AI is doing the same thing from the supply side.

Global Capability Centres are accelerating the shift. According to Nasscom and Zinnov's 2026 report, India now hosts 2,117 GCCs employing 2.36 million professionals and generating $98.4 billion in revenue. Over 1,200 of those centres have embedded AI and machine learning capabilities. The work is staying in India — but increasingly, it is being done by machines rather than people.

Chandrasekaran offered a silver lining. "Far from being a mortal threat, AI is the most significant opportunity yet for enterprise IT," he said. He pointed to five growth areas: modernising legacy systems, redesigning business processes, managing AI governance, sovereign AI, and physical AI applications.

But the numbers tell a harder story. TCS spent ₹1,260 crore on restructuring in the last fiscal year. It shed 26,000 workers against a plan to lose 1,200. And its chairman just told the world that AI agents will match the human headcount within three years.

The era of mass hiring in Indian IT is not ending sometime in the future. It ended last year. The industry is only now beginning to say it out loud.
